title: The history of work and power
tagline: From Archimedes' lever to the star label on your AC: how people learned that force times distance is something you can measure, sell and pay for.
intro: For two thousand years people used levers and pulleys without a word for what they traded. Galileo saw that a machine gains force only by losing distance, engineers measured horses and water wheels, and in 1829 Coriolis and Poncelet gave the idea its name: work. Joule showed that work and heat are the same stuff, the watt and the joule became units, and meters began to charge homes for every kilowatt-hour.

eras.name: Machines and the golden rule
eras.summary: Greek engineers explain the lever and the pulley, and Galileo sees the catch: what a machine gains in force it loses in distance.

eras.name: Measuring a day's work
eras.summary: Engineers selling pumps and mills compare them with horses and measure weight raised times height, per minute.

eras.name: Work gets a name
eras.summary: French engineers call force times distance 'travail', and Joule shows that work and heat are two faces of one thing.

eras.name: Units, meters and bills
eras.summary: The watt and the joule become units, meters count kilowatt-hours, and star labels help families pick appliances that do the same job with less energy.

events.title: The law of the lever
events.text: In On the Equilibrium of Planes, Archimedes proved that weights balance on a lever when weight times distance from the pivot is the same on both sides. A later writer, Pappus, credits him with the boast: give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.
events.why: It is the first exact rule for trading a small force for a big one.

events.title: Five machines to move a load
events.text: Hero's Mechanics lists five devices for moving heavy loads: the lever, the windlass, the pulley, the wedge and the screw. He explained them with balanced forces, but had no idea yet of work.
events.why: These are still the simple machines taught in school today.

events.title: You can't cheat nature
events.text: Teaching at Padua, Galileo wrote Le Mecaniche, a short book on levers, pulleys, screws and ramps. He showed they all follow one rule: a machine that lets a small force lift a big weight makes that force move much further. Marin Mersenne printed it in French in 1634.
events.why: It is the first clear statement that machines transform effort but never create it.

events.title: Weight times height
events.text: In a letter explaining machines to Constantijn Huygens, Descartes wrote that lifting 100 pounds one foot twice is the same as lifting 200 pounds one foot, or 100 pounds two feet. The effort of a job is weight multiplied by height.
events.why: It measures a machine's job the way we measure work today.

events.title: As many horses as it replaces
events.text: In The Miner's Friend, Savery sold his steam pump for draining mines by saying how many horses it could replace. Mine owners paid for horses, so a horse was a unit they understood.
events.why: Comparing engines with horses led to the horsepower.

events.title: Testing water wheels
events.text: Smeaton spent seven years testing model water wheels and windmills and reported how much weight each could raise, how high, in a given time. He showed that an overshot wheel, fed from the top, does far more work than an undershot one. The Royal Society gave him its Copley Medal.
events.why: Measuring weight raised times height per minute is measuring power.

events.title: One horsepower
events.text: Watt watched mill horses turn a wheel of 12 ft radius 144 times an hour, pulling with about 180 pounds-force. That came to about 32,600 foot-pounds a minute. In 1783 he and Boulton rounded it up to 33,000: one horsepower, today 745.7 W.
events.why: It gave buyers a number for how fast an engine could work.

events.title: The motive power of fire
events.text: Carnot asked how much work a steam engine could possibly get from its fuel. He found a limit set by how hot and how cold its two ends are, so no heat engine can turn all its heat into work.
events.why: It explains why a petrol engine is only about 30% efficient.

events.title: Travail: work gets its name
events.text: In Du calcul de l'effet des machines, Coriolis called force times distance moved 'travail', work. He also put the half into ½ m v², showing that the work done on a body equals the change in its energy of motion. He even proposed a unit, the dynamode, 1,000 kilogram-metres, which never caught on.
events.why: Work became a precise, measurable quantity for engineers.

events.title: Mechanics for the factory
events.text: Teaching engineers and workers at Metz, Poncelet used 'mechanical work' as the key idea for judging machines, independently of Coriolis. His Introduction à la mécanique industrielle came out in 1829, and he also designed better water wheels.
events.why: He made work the everyday language of engineering.

events.title: The paddle wheel
events.text: Joule let falling weights spin a paddle wheel in an insulated can of water and measured how much the water warmed. The same amount of work always gave the same amount of heat: 819 foot-pounds per British thermal unit in 1845, refined to about 772 by 1850.
events.why: It proved that work and heat are both energy, which is why the unit of work is the joule.

events.title: A unit called the watt
events.text: In his presidential address to the British Association, Siemens proposed naming the practical unit of electrical power after James Watt.
events.why: It joined the steam age and the electric age in one unit.

events.title: A meter for AC
events.text: Working for Westinghouse, Shallenberger noticed a loose spring turning in the magnetic field of an AC lamp. He turned the idea into a meter that measured how much alternating current a customer used. About 120,000 were sold within ten years.
events.why: Homes could now be charged for the energy they used, not a flat fee per lamp.

events.title: The joule and the watt made official
events.text: Meeting during the Paris World's Fair, the congress adopted the joule for work and the watt, one joule per second, for power. Joule died in October that year, weeks after his unit became official.
events.why: Scientists and engineers everywhere could now use the same words for work and power.

events.title: The kilowatt-hour meter
events.text: Bláthy's induction meter, shown at the Frankfurt Fair, used a spinning disc to add up power over time and show kilowatt-hours. The same principle ran most electricity meters for the next hundred years.
events.why: The kilowatt-hour became the unit on every electricity bill.

events.title: Joule and watt join the SI
events.who: 11th General Conference on Weights and Measures
events.text: The new International System of Units, the SI, made the joule (a newton times a metre) its unit of energy and work, and the watt (a joule per second) its unit of power.
events.why: One set of units now serves physics, engineering and your electricity bill.

events.title: Weighing with watts
events.text: At the National Physical Laboratory, Kibble designed a balance that compares mechanical power, a mass moving in gravity, with electrical power in a coil. It was called the watt balance.
events.why: Power became precise enough to define the kilogram itself.

events.title: Pedalling across the Channel
events.where: Folkestone, England to Cap Gris-Nez, France
events.text: Cyclist Bryan Allen pedalled the Gossamer Albatross 35.7 km across the English Channel in 2 hours 49 minutes, producing about 300 W, just enough to keep the ultralight plane in the air.
events.why: It shows how much a fit person can do with a few hundred watts.

events.title: India's star labels
events.text: Under the Energy Conservation Act 2001, the BEE launched its star labels: one to five stars showing how many units a year an appliance needs. From 7 January 2010 labels became mandatory for frost-free fridges, room ACs, tube lights and distribution transformers.
events.why: Families could compare the energy bill before buying, not after.

events.title: The kilogram, by way of the watt
events.who: General Conference on Weights and Measures
events.text: The kilogram stopped being a metal cylinder in a vault. It is now fixed by the Planck constant, and Kibble balances, renamed after Bryan Kibble in 2016, realise it by balancing mechanical and electrical power.
events.why: A unit of mass now rests on measuring watts.

people.name: James Watt

people.name: Sadi Carnot

people.name: Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis
people.note: Named work 'travail' and wrote kinetic energy as ½ m v².

people.name: Jean-Victor Poncelet
people.note: Made mechanical work the language of industrial engineering.

people.name: James Prescott Joule
people.note: Measured how much heat a given amount of work makes.

people.name: Bryan Kibble
people.note: Invented the watt balance that now helps define the kilogram.

facts: Watt measured about 32,600 foot-pounds a minute for a mill horse, then rounded up to 33,000, perhaps so that buyers of his engines would never feel short-changed.
Europe and India often quote engines in metric horsepower (PS), 735.5 W, about 1.4% smaller than Watt's 745.7 W.
One kilowatt-hour, a single unit on your bill, is 3.6 million joules: enough to lift a 1,000 kg car about 367 m.
Joule died on 11 October 1889, weeks after the unit named after him was officially adopted.
Coriolis also proposed a unit of work, the dynamode, 1,000 kilogram-metres. Nobody used it.
